# Postmortem: Four-hour checkout outage from connection pool exhaustion

**Date of incident:** 2026-10-06 · **Duration:** 4h 00m (13:44–17:44 UTC) · **Severity:** SEV1 · **Status:** Resolved, remediations in progress

## Summary

On 2026-10-06, `checkout-api` failed most requests for four hours. A deploy of the downstream `fraud-scoring` service raised its p99 latency from 120 ms to 28 s. `checkout-api` calls `fraud-scoring` inside a database transaction with no HTTP timeout, so every in-flight checkout held a database connection while it waited. The connection pool on every pod filled within six minutes, and all endpoints sharing that pool failed, including ones that never call `fraud-scoring`.

The outage lasted four hours mainly because responders spent the first two and a half investigating the database, which was healthy.

## Impact

- About 94% of `checkout-api` requests failed or timed out at peak, across checkout, cart and order-status endpoints.
- About 18,400 checkout attempts failed. Revenue impact: [to be confirmed by finance].
- `order-history` was degraded for 20 minutes (14:50–15:10) as a side effect of a mitigation attempt.
- No data was lost or corrupted. Failed transactions rolled back cleanly.

## Timeline (UTC)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 13:38 | `fraud-scoring` v2.31 deployed. A new rule queries an unindexed table. p99 latency starts climbing. |
| 13:44 | Database pool reaches 40/40 in use on all 12 `checkout-api` pods. **Outage begins.** |
| 13:47 | Alert fires: `checkout-api` 5xx rate above 5%. On-call paged. |
| 13:52 | On-call acknowledges. Logs show `HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms`. Database suspected. |
| 14:05 | SEV1 declared. Database team paged. |
| 14:20 | Database team reports the primary is healthy at 15% CPU, with 480 of 500 connections in use, mostly `idle in transaction`. |
| 14:35 | Rolling restart of `checkout-api`. Service recovers for about 90 seconds, then pools saturate again. |
| 14:50 | `checkout-api` scaled from 12 to 20 pods. Potential demand (20 × 40 = 800) exceeds `max_connections` (500). New pods fail with `FATAL: too many connections` and `order-history` starts losing connections. |
| 15:10 | Scaled back to 12 pods. `order-history` recovers. |
| 15:25 | Database failover attempted on the theory of a stuck primary. No change. |
| 16:10 | Thread dump shows 38 of 40 worker threads per pod holding a connection while blocked on a socket read in `FraudClient.score()`. |
| 16:20 | `fraud-scoring` team paged. They confirm elevated latency since the 13:38 deploy. No alert fired on their side. |
| 16:40 | Rollback of `fraud-scoring` v2.31 started. |
| 17:05 | Rollback complete. `fraud-scoring` p99 returns to 130 ms. |
| 17:10 | `checkout-api` pools still saturated by threads stuck on old sockets. Rolling restart started. |
| 17:25 | `checkout-api` error rate below 1%. |
| 17:44 | Backlog of retried payment webhooks drained. **Incident resolved.** |

## Root cause

`OrderService.placeOrder()` is annotated `@Transactional`, so it takes a database connection on entry and holds it until return. Inside that method it makes a synchronous HTTP call to `fraud-scoring`. The HTTP client was built with library defaults, which means no read timeout.

In normal operation each request holds its connection for about 150 ms. At 25 requests per second per pod, that is roughly 4 connections in use out of 40. When `fraud-scoring` latency rose to 28 s, the same traffic needed about 700 connections per pod. The pool was exhausted in minutes, and every later request waited 30 s for a connection and then failed.

Two design properties turned a slow dependency into a full outage:

1. **One shared pool.** All endpoints draw from the same pool, so cart and order-status requests failed even though they never call `fraud-scoring`.
2. **Shallow health checks.** `/healthz` does not touch the pool, so Kubernetes kept all pods in rotation and never restarted them.

## Contributing factors

- **Misleading signal.** The only visible error named the database pool. Nothing pointed at the downstream call until someone took a thread dump, 2h 26m into the outage.
- **No per-dependency latency dashboard or alert** in `checkout-api`. The latency increase in `fraud-scoring` was visible only in that team's own metrics.
- **`fraud-scoring` alerts on error rate only.** It was slow but returning 200s, so its owners were not paged.
- **No circuit breaker or kill switch** for the fraud call. The only mitigation available was fixing `fraud-scoring` itself.
- **Client retries.** The mobile app retries failed checkouts three times without backoff, which multiplied load on an already saturated pool.
- **The scaling runbook did not mention `max_connections`.** Scaling out widened the blast radius to `order-history`.
- **No deploy correlation.** The `fraud-scoring` deploy at 13:38 was not shown on the `checkout-api` dashboard or in the incident channel.

## What went well

- The alert fired three minutes after the outage began, and the on-call acknowledged within five.
- The scale-out mistake was recognised and reverted in 20 minutes.
- Once the thread dump identified the blocked call, the right team was engaged within 10 minutes.

## What went poorly

- Two and a half hours were spent on the database on the strength of one log line.
- Restarting gave a 90-second recovery, which was a strong hint of an external cause that nobody followed up.
- Two mitigations (scale-out, failover) were applied without a hypothesis for why they would help.

## Remediations

| # | Action | Owner | Priority | Due |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Set connect (500 ms) and read (2 s) timeouts on the `fraud-scoring` client. Audit all other outbound clients in `checkout-api` for missing timeouts. | Checkout | P0 | 2026-10-13 |
| 2 | Move the `fraud-scoring` call outside the transaction so no database connection is held during network I/O. | Checkout | P0 | 2026-10-20 |
| 3 | Add a circuit breaker on the fraud call, with a product-approved fallback (queue for manual review above a threshold amount). | Checkout, Risk | P1 | 2026-11-03 |
| 4 | Add a runtime kill switch for the fraud call. | Checkout | P1 | 2026-10-27 |
| 5 | Split the pool so checkout writes cannot starve read-only endpoints. | Checkout | P1 | 2026-11-10 |
| 6 | Add p99 latency alerts to `fraud-scoring`, and a per-dependency latency panel and alert to `checkout-api`. | Fraud, Checkout | P1 | 2026-10-20 |
| 7 | Alert on pool wait time and active-connection hold time, with the runbook linking to a thread-dump procedure. | Checkout | P1 | 2026-10-20 |
| 8 | Add the missing index, and add a query-plan check to the `fraud-scoring` rule review. | Fraud | P1 | 2026-10-15 |
| 9 | Add exponential backoff with jitter to mobile checkout retries. | Mobile | P2 | 2026-11-17 |
| 10 | Update the scaling runbook with the `max_connections` budget, and add a guard that blocks scale-out beyond it. | Platform | P2 | 2026-11-03 |
| 11 | Show upstream and downstream deploys as annotations on service dashboards. | Platform | P2 | 2026-11-17 |
| 12 | Add a lint rule that flags HTTP calls inside `@Transactional` methods. | Platform | P2 | 2026-11-24 |

Items 1 and 2 each prevent a recurrence on their own. Items 3 to 5 limit the blast radius of the next slow dependency. Items 6, 7 and 11 would have cut diagnosis from two and a half hours to minutes.
